summary.title: Don't repeat yourself - Wikipedia
summary.one_liner: DRY is the principle that every piece of knowledge should have a single authoritative representation, and it is contrasted with the WET and AHA approaches.
keywords: prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction
andy hunt dave thomas pragmatic programmer
takeaways: DRY means every piece of knowledge should have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation in a system.
Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas formulated DRY in The Pragmatic Programmer, applying it to schemas, tests, build systems and docs.
Bertrand Meyer's single choice principle says one module should know the exhaustive list of alternatives a system supports.
WET (write everything twice) is the opposing view, where the same information is repeated across layers.
AHA (avoid hasty abstractions) argues for delaying abstraction until it is needed, following the phrase 'prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction'.
summary.summary: This Wikipedia article defines the Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY) principle of software development, which aims to reduce repeated information likely to change, using abstractions or data normalization. It covers the origin of the principle in Hunt and Thomas's The Pragmatic Programmer, Bertrand Meyer's single choice principle, and the opposing WET approach. It also describes AHA programming, which advises avoiding premature abstraction, and lists related concepts and external references.
